title: Deterministic Verification and a Single‑Repair Guardrail for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations: a Paired, Shared‑Candidate Study
abstract: We report a sealed, preregistered paired experiment that measured the marginal verifier-detected effect of interposing a deterministic validator plus at most one automated repair on the same LLM-generated configuration candidate. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial generation call per intent; that identical candidate reused for both baseline and guarded episodes) we generated one candidate per natural-language intent with gpt-5-mini for N = 250 pairs and evaluated two episodes per intent: baseline (accept candidate) and guarded (deterministic_netops_validator_v5; if failing, permit one automated repair). Execution completed 500 episodes with model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial generations + 1 repair). Results: baseline verifier-pass 249/250 (99.6%), guarded verifier-pass 250/250 (100.0%); contingency n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = +0.4 percentage points, 95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp] (paired bootstrap percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered sim‑to‑real (production-like) confirmatory contrast was not executed; the reported inferential estimand applies only to the synthetic/emulation partition executed here. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived and referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being explored as intent‑to‑configuration translators in network operations (NetOps), promising faster authoring of device CLI sequences and intent‑driven automation. Stochastic generation, however, creates operational risk: syntax errors, incorrect command ordering, local‑policy violations, and vendor‑CLI subtleties can produce unsafe or non‑functional device changes. Prior survey and empirical work document LLM feasibility for draft configurations while highlighting the continuing need for deterministic verification or human oversight [1],[2].

A common architectural mitigation is to interpose a deterministic validator between generation and acceptance and to permit bounded automated repairs when validator checks fail (generate–verify–repair, GVR). Existing reports show such pipelines reduce mechanically verifiable error classes (syntax, ordering, local policy) but do not settle the marginal benefit of adding a validator+single repair when modern LLM outputs already conform to validator encodings under constrained tasks [3],[4].

This paper reports a preregistered, artifact‑backed paired experiment explicitly designed under shared_initial_candidate semantics. That design reuses the identical initial LLM candidate for both baseline and guarded conditions and therefore isolates the marginal effect of deterministic validation and a single permitted repair on identical model outputs. Our principal, evidence‑grounded contribution is the exact quantification of that marginal verifier‑detected improvement (point estimate and uncertainty bounds) for a constrained NetOps task bank executed in an emulation-style partition.
sections.related_work:
Survey and experimental literature motivate validator‑centric pipelines and evaluation rigor. Work on LLMs for NetOps documents multiple prototype systems and benchmarks for intent‑driven configuration generation and highlights frequent reliance on emulation or synthetic tasks for evaluation [1],[5]. Generate–verify and generate–repair architectures—applied both in program repair and in configuration domains—are a recurring mitigation pattern that improves detection and automated correction of mechanically checkable defects, though deeper semantic correctness and cross‑vendor subtleties remain challenging [3],[4],[6].

Deterministic network‑verification tools (e.g., Batfish and header‑space techniques) provide established mechanized checks for forwarding, reachability, and many local‑policy constraints; these tools are natural validators in GVR pipelines but trade off modelling fidelity and integration complexity [7],[8]. Security analyses of prompt‑injection and retrieval‑based threats emphasize the need for filtering and validation but indicate adaptive adversaries are an unresolved operational threat [9].

This study differs by (i) using a preregistered paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics to measure the validator+single‑repair marginal effect on identical candidates, (ii) reporting reconciled provider‑call accounting and stage_counts so model_call decomposition is auditable, and (iii) archiving validator traces and reconciliation artifacts for reproducibility.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered study-cand-2026-LLM-verifier-sim2real-v1. The confirmatory design was paired with N_pairs = 250 and shared_initial_candidate generation_semantics; primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistration fixed the one‑repair policy, exclusion and contamination rules, the exact analysis tests (exact McNemar two‑sided plus paired‑bootstrap CIs), and the maximum model‑call budget. Preregistration SHA‑256: 7a984dbf7265c9a774eaf95c6c930dcf5f1e8845088bbc0e0855e3b4f1000ede.

Explicit shared_initial_candidate paragraph (required). Under the registered shared_initial_candidate semantics exactly one initial model‑generation call was produced per intent; that identical generated candidate was reused for both episodes (baseline and guarded). No independent first‑pass generation per condition was performed. Provider accounting reconciles model_calls_used = 251, decomposed as 250 shared_initial_generation calls plus 1 repair call; stage_counts recorded by the adapter are {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1}. The adapter labels used in audit fields (e.g., condition_counts: {"shared":250, "guarded":1}) reflect recording conventions and do not indicate independent guarded first‑pass generations. Deterministic reconciliation artifacts (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) contain the per‑stage mapping and provider_call_audit used for this decomposition.

Task generation and constraints. A deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 250 constrained intent tasks. Each task specified initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, workflow policies (make‑before‑break, all_down_before_change, group activity constraints), and a difficulty label (medium/hard/very_hard). Tasks focused on workflow‑sensitive changes (uplink switchover, paired MTU changes, rolling VLAN migrations) and preserved protected interfaces.

Model invocation and guarded pipeline. The declared model for initial generation was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json). For each intent one shared initial generation call produced the candidate. The guarded pipeline submitted that candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5, which performs full_intent_constraint_validation: parsing CLI sequences, checking required_sequence ordering, enforcing workflow constraints, computing a final_state snapshot, and returning a boolean valid flag and detailed violation codes. If valid = false the pipeline permitted up to one deterministic, template‑driven repair attempt (e.g., syntactic re‑ordering to match required_sequence, splitting/joining commands) and re‑submitted the repaired candidate to the validator. No multi‑iteration repairs or human escalations were permitted by design.

Inclusion, contamination, and missingness. Exclusion rules removed items that failed vendor parsers preventing deterministic verification or contained credential‑like tokens or denylist hits. Contamination detectors flagged instruction‑like embedded tokens or private‑address artifacts; flagged items were to be excluded from the primary analysis and treated in sensitivity analyses. In the executed confirmatory partition no episodes were excluded or flagged and complete_pair_count = 250.

Analysis plan and exact procedures. The preregistered analysis executor was paired_binary_analysis_v1. The primary hypothesis test was the exact two‑sided McNemar on paired outcomes (discordant counts), and we computed a paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the guarded − baseline difference using 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). All analysis inputs, scripts, and outputs are archived.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and reconciliation. Execution completed planned_episode_count = 500 (250 pairs × 2 episodes) with completed_episode_count = 500 and failed_episode_count = 0. Provider accounting reconciled model_calls_used = 251; stage_counts reported by the adapter are {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1}. The single extra model call beyond 250 corresponds to one repair attempt exercised by the guarded pipeline.

Primary outcomes and contingency. Validator‑scored successes: baseline_success_count = 249 (baseline_success_rate = 0.996), guarded_success_count = 250 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). Paired contingency: n11 = 249, n10 = 1 (guarded=1 baseline=0), n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The only discordant pair corresponds to the single exercised repair; repair‑conversion rate on the confirmatory partition = 1/250 = 0.4%.

Statistical inference. Exact McNemar two‑sided test on discordant counts (n10 = 1, n01 = 0) yields p = 1.0. Paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI for guarded − baseline (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.012] (i.e., 0–1.2 percentage points). All numeric analysis artifacts (contingency table CSV, condition summary, bootstrap parameters and logs) are archived.

Validator diagnostics and representative artifacts. Passed episodes report parsed_command_count equal to required_command_count (example: task‑000003 had parsed_command_count = required_command_count = 6 and valid = true). Representative raw responses, normalized configurations, and validator traces for sample tasks are preserved in the execution scoring artifacts and referenced in the evidence bundle. Contamination detectors flagged no episodes in the confirmatory partition.

Repair exercise. Exactly one repair call occurred and converted the sole failing candidate into a validator pass; no other repairs were needed in the confirmatory partition.
sections.discussion:
Interpreting the near‑null marginal verifier effect. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics and the constrained synthetic/emulation partition, the marginal verifier‑detected benefit of adding a deterministic validator plus one automated repair was small: initial gpt‑5‑mini candidates satisfied the deterministic validator in 249/250 tasks; the guarded pipeline converted the single failing candidate via the single permitted repair. The paired‑bootstrap CI upper bound (1.2 percentage points) empirically bounds the maximum plausible verifier improvement for this task scope.

Artifact‑grounded reasons for the small observed effect. Three artifact‑supported factors explain the small guarded gain: (1) the deterministic task generator encoded constrained intents and allowed_touched_fields that reduce ambiguity and favor well‑formed CLI sequences; (2) gpt‑5‑mini produced highly consistent, syntactically well‑formed sequences for these constrained tasks; and (3) the deterministic validator checks mechanically verifiable properties (syntax, command ordering, final_state snapshot) and does not capture broader live protocol correctness or emergent cross‑device behavior.

Power and preregistration assumptions. The preregistered power calculation assumed a baseline pass rate ≈ 0.90 to target detection of a 15 percentage‑point effect; the realized baseline pass rate (0.996) is substantially higher than assumed and reduces power to detect small absolute improvements. Consequently, the paired‑bootstrap CI is the most informative practical summary of the plausible verifier benefit under executed conditions.

Threats to validity and scope. Internal validity: results depend on prompt templates, single‑repair policy, and shared_initial_candidate semantics. Construct validity: the deterministic validator measures mechanically verifiable correctness (syntax, required_sequence, final_state snapshot) but does not assert live protocol‑level or emergent behavioral correctness. External validity: the confirmatory evidence covers only the synthetic/emulation partition; preregistered community and production‑like partitions were not executed. Security: adaptive prompt‑injection and retrieval‑based adversaries were not exercised and remain open threats.

Operational implications (bounded). In tightly constrained emulation‑style tasks with a capable LLM the marginal verifier‑detected improvement from a single repair may be small; this finding does not generalize to broader or adversarial operational contexts where validators with broader checks, multi‑iteration repair, human escalation, or highly heterogeneous vendor targets could produce materially different benefits.
sections.conclusion: We executed a sealed, preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics to measure the verifier‑detected marginal effect of deterministic validation plus one permitted automated repair on identical LLM‑generated configuration candidates. For N = 250 constrained synthetic intent tasks, initial gpt‑5‑mini candidates passed the deterministic validator in 249/250 cases; the guarded pipeline converted the single failing candidate via the single permitted repair. Observed paired improvement = 0.4 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp]; p = 1.0). We explicitly disclose that the preregistered sim‑to‑real confirmatory contrast was not executed and that the executed confirmatory estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on the synthetic/emulation partition only. Broader production, adversarial, multi‑model, and multi‑iteration repair evaluations remain necessary to establish generality. All execution manifests, raw responses, validator traces, repair traces, and analysis artifacts referenced in this paper are archived and available in the evidence bundle described in the Disclosure Statement.

disclosure_statement:
Human role and autonomy boundary: after an autonomy lock required by the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track, the autonomous system performed literature search, study selection, preregistration freeze, prompt preservation, model calls, deterministic validation, permitted repair execution, analysis, drafting, peer‑review, revision, and finalization without manual human editing of technical content. A human Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and performed pre‑lock infrastructure development only.

Models, tools, and execution summary: declared model = gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses); deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; deterministic task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Execution used a guarded generate–verify–repair flow permitting at most one automated repair per episode. Confirmatory execution results reported here are from the synthetic/emulation partition only: planned_episode_count = 500, completed_episode_count = 500, complete_pair_count = 250, model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial_generation + 1 repair), stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1}. Preregistration study id = study-cand-2026-LLM-verifier-sim2real-v1 (preregistration SHA-256: 7a984dbf7265c9a774eaf95c6c930dcf5f1e8845088bbc0e0855e3b4f1000ede). Immutable master prompt used to initiate the autonomous run is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA-256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba).

Artifact bundle pointer for reproducibility: the full execution and analysis manifests, raw responses, validator traces, repair traces, and per‑artifact hashes are archived in the evidence bundle; a single archive manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) enumerates the full artifact list and hashes and is the authoritative machine‑readable pointer for reproduction and audit. The manifest and the preregistration artifact together contain the detailed per‑file provenance referenced above.
limitations: Confirmatory scope limited to the synthetic/emulation partition; preregistered community and production-like partitions were not executed.
Deterministic validator assessed mechanically verifiable properties (syntax and prescribed workflow sequences) and did not measure protocol dynamics or emergent cross‑device behavior.
Single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and one validator implementation were used; results do not establish multi‑model or alternate‑validator generality.
Only one automated repair attempt was permitted by design; multi‑iteration repairs or human‑in‑the‑loop escalation were not evaluated.
Adversarial and retrieval‑based attacks (adaptive prompt‑injection, vendor‑targeted exploit vectors) and large‑scale production heterogeneity were not exercised and remain open threats.
